opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing you have to ask is: what does "safe" even mean? People use the word as if we all agree on a definition, and we don't. So when I look at it, I try to break it into concrete capabilities, the specific tools we'd need, and then ask whether each one is actually achievable.

You'd want to be able to **explain** the system: understand why it made a decision, not just get a post-hoc story. You'd want to **predict** what it's going to do before it does it. You'd want to **verify** its behavior, ideally with something like a mathematical proof that it will always act within certain bounds. And ultimately you'd want to **control** it: to correct it, modify it, or turn it off if something goes wrong.

What I found, looking at each of those, is that there are fundamental limits. Take explainability. If a system is smarter than you, any explanation it gives is either a simplification, a lossy compression you can understand but which isn't the full picture, or the full picture, which you can't comprehend. Either way, you don't really understand it.

Predictability is similar. If you could perfectly predict what a superintelligent system would do, you'd essentially be as smart as it is. The whole point of building something more capable than us is that it comes up with solutions we didn't think of. That's the value, and it's also the danger.

Verification has its own problem. You can verify a proof, but you need a verifier, which is software, which needs its own verification. You get an infinite regress. You can get very high confidence, but not 100%. And for a system that makes billions of decisions, a one-in-a-million error rate isn't comforting.

Then there's control, which people assume is solvable as an engineering problem. I don't think it is, not indefinitely. You can control a narrow system. But a general system that's more capable than you, operating in a complex, open-ended environment, keeps finding new ways around whatever constraints you put on it. Safety isn't something you achieve once. It's a perpetual problem, and you have to win every single time while the system only has to get it wrong once.

So when someone tells me they have a plan for safe superintelligence, my first question is: which of these capabilities do you have, and can you show me it's actually possible? Usually the answer is, "We'll figure it out." That's not a safety plan. That's hope.

r001.rationale: The response says we would want to predict what a system will do, but does not distinguish predicting intermediate steps from predicting only its terminal goal.

r002.rationale: It says people disagree about what “safe” means, but does not identify ambiguity in human language as a danger when communicating with AI systems.

r003.rationale: It discusses limits involving explainability, predictability, verification, and control, but does not identify insufficient human research capacity as a bottleneck to assessing which impossibility results matter for AI safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we don't know, and that's the uncomfortable part. When people talk about safety capabilities, they usually mean things like interpretability, control, alignment, verification. And I take all of those seriously. But if you look at each of them individually, they're all unsolved problems, and some of them may not be solvable at all for systems that are smarter than us.

Take explainability. For a system to be safe, I'd want to understand why it's making a decision. But if the system is genuinely superintelligent, its explanation might be either a simplification I can follow, which means I'm not actually seeing the real reasoning, or the real reasoning, which I can't follow. There's no third option where I both understand it fully and it's operating beyond my level.

Then there's predictability. Safety basically means I can predict that the system won't do something catastrophic. But if I could predict exactly what a superintelligent system would do, I would be that smart myself. Unpredictability is almost a definition of what it means for something to be more intelligent than you.

And control. People talk about an off switch, about boxing, about oversight. But every one of those assumes the system is not actively trying to get around them, and if it's more capable than you, it will find paths you didn't anticipate. We've seen this already in small ways with reward hacking in simple reinforcement learning agents. Scale that up and it's not reassuring.

So when you ask what concrete capabilities are needed, my answer is that we'd need capabilities we don't currently have, and I have serious doubts that we can get them before we get the systems themselves. That's why I lean toward the view that the only genuinely safe move is not building things we can't understand or control, rather than hoping we'll figure out the safety part afterward. In every other engineering discipline you don't deploy something and then start working out how to make it safe. Here, that's essentially the plan.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predicting a superintelligent system’s behavior generally, but does not say prediction must cover intermediate steps rather than only its terminal goal.

r002.rationale: It does not identify ambiguity in human language as a danger when communicating with AI systems.

r003.rationale: It says safety capabilities are unsolved and may be unobtainable in time, but does not identify limited human research capacity to determine which impossibility results apply to AI safety.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate making a system more useful from making it safe. A system can be very capable, follow instructions well, and still do something dangerous because the instructions fail to capture what we actually wanted.

Concretely, you would want to understand why it makes decisions, predict the consequences of its actions, constrain what it can do, and intervene when something goes wrong. You would also want those protections to survive learning, updates, and situations you didn’t anticipate.

The difficulty is that each of those is a separate research problem. Explaining an answer is not the same as faithfully explaining the process that produced it. Passing safety tests is not the same as being safe outside the test environment. And having a shutdown button helps only if the system cannot prevent you from using it.

So I would ask: safe within what boundaries, against which failures, and with what evidence? For a narrowly defined system, we can make meaningful progress. For a system that can act across the world and outthink the people supervising it, we don’t yet have a convincing way to establish those guarantees.

r001.rationale: It mentions predicting consequences and explaining the process behind decisions, but does not say safety prediction must cover intermediate steps rather than only the terminal goal.

r002.rationale: It says instructions may fail to capture what people want, but does not identify ambiguity in human language as a danger in communicating with AI.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss limited human research capacity or determining which impossibility results apply to AI safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate making a system more capable from making it safe. A system can understand what you want, predict the consequences of its actions, and still do something you would not approve of. Intelligence alone doesn't give us that guarantee.

So you need to specify what safety means, verify that the system satisfies that specification, and make sure the guarantee survives learning, self-modification, and interaction with the real world. Each of those is a very difficult problem. Even specifying what we want is difficult, because people disagree, and our preferences change.

And then there is control. Can you detect when the system is doing something dangerous? Can you intervene? Can you shut it down? Those capabilities are useful, but if the system is more capable than the people monitoring it, you have to explain why it cannot circumvent them. That's where I become skeptical of claims that we know how to make a superintelligent system safe.
